title: Shannon's Sampling Theorem: Why Sample Faster Than Twice the Highest Frequency?

paper.title: Communication in the Presence of Noise

hook: A sine wave sampled too slowly looks like a slower sine wave. This is aliasing. Shannon's theorem tells us how fast we must sample to avoid it.

symbols.meaning: Integer that brings f - k f_s into [-f_s/2, f_s/2]

equation.caption: The apparent frequency after sampling. If f_s > 2f, then k=0 and f_a = f (no aliasing).

steps: The signal is \(x(t) = \sin(2\pi f t)\) with \(f = {{f}}\) Hz.
The sampling rate is \(f_s = {{fs}}\) Hz, so samples are taken every \(1/f_s\) seconds.
If \(f_s > 2f\), the samples can be used to reconstruct the original frequency \(f\).
If \(f_s < 2f\), the samples appear to come from a lower frequency \(f_a = |f - k f_s|\), where \(k = \mathrm{round}(f/f_s)\).

explorations.title: No aliasing when sampling above Nyquist rate
explorations.predict: Set f = 3 Hz and f_s = 10 Hz. Is f_s > 2f? What is the alias frequency?
explorations.observe: The reconstructed curve matches the original. The alias frequency equals 3 Hz.
explorations.why: Because f_s > 2f, k = round(3/10) = 0, so f_a = |3 - 0*10| = 3 Hz. The samples capture the true frequency.

explorations.title: Aliasing when sampling below Nyquist rate
explorations.predict: Set f = 7 Hz and f_s = 10 Hz. Is f_s < 2f? What alias frequency do you expect?
explorations.observe: The reconstructed curve is a slower sine wave at 3 Hz. The samples lie on this slower wave.
explorations.why: Because f_s < 2f, k = round(7/10) = 1, so f_a = |7 - 1*10| = 3 Hz. The samples cannot distinguish 7 Hz from 3 Hz at this sampling rate.

self_tests.name: No aliasing at exactly Nyquist rate
Aliasing when f_s is half of f

limitation: This demonstration uses a single sine wave. Real signals contain many frequencies, and aliasing occurs if any component exceeds f_s/2. Also, perfect reconstruction requires an ideal low-pass filter, which is not physically realizable.
misconception: Sampling faster than the highest frequency is not enough; you must sample faster than twice the highest frequency. Also, aliasing does not just lose information—it creates false lower frequencies that were not in the original signal.

claims.text: A signal must be sampled at a rate greater than twice its highest frequency to avoid aliasing.
When sampling below the Nyquist rate, the apparent frequency is |f - k f_s| with k = round(f/f_s).
The toy model uses a single sine wave and ideal sampling; it ignores noise, quantization, and filter effects.

outcomes.outcome: Explain why the sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency.
Calculate the alias frequency when sampling below the Nyquist rate.
Interpret the time-domain plot to see aliasing.
